title: Hurricane Nolo continues to strengthen as it unleashes heavy rain on Hawaii | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Heavy rain from Hurricane Nolo is ramping up in southern Hawaii, the islands’ third dangerous brush with a hurricane in just six weeks. Potentially life-threatening flooding and mudslides are again possible as the state contends with a Pacific tropical season supercharged by this year’ssuper El Niño.

Nolo rapidly intensified into a Category 2 hurricane Friday and remained at that strength on Saturday morning. Rapid intensification is an increase in maximum sustained wind speeds of at least 35 mph in 24 hours or less, and it’shappening more frequentlyin a world warming due to fossil fuel pollution.

The Big Island will see the worst of Nolo’s impacts as it continues to strengthen and makes its closest approach Saturday local time. Extreme rain is its most serious threat, but Nolo is also whipping up strong wind gusts and dangerous seas.

Hurricane Lalatook a similarly close track to the Big Island in mid-August as a Category 1 storm and unleashed catastrophic flooding there. On the other side of the state,Hurricane Lowelldelivered a blow to Kauai and Niihau in early September as a Category 2 storm.

Hawaii Gov. Josh Green hasdeclareda state of emergency, the third storm-related emergency declaration this month, in anticipation of the storm’s impacts. And President Donald Trump approved the state’s request for a pre-landfall Presidential Emergency Declaration, Greensaid Friday.

Nolo is expected to make its closest approach to the Big Island as a high-end Category 2 hurricane or a Category 3 major hurricane.

Nolo’s rainbands continue to spin into the Big Island and they will spread to Maui, Lanai and Molokai on Saturday.

Rainfall totals have lowered with the most recent forecast, but a dangerous amount is still possible.

Eight to 12 inches of rain are possible over eastern and southern portions of the Big Island through Sunday, with up to 16 inches in the steepest terrain, according to the National Hurricane Center. Last month, the Big Island’s steep mountains helped wring more than 40 inches of rain out of Hurricane Lala’s bands, unleashing catastrophic flash flooding from which the island is still recovering.

Nolo’s rainfall is expected to be lower, but still significant on the western side of the island, with up to 6 inches possible.

In eastern Maui, 4 to 6 inches are possible with isolated amounts up to 8 inches. About 1 to 3 inches of rain are expected elsewhere on the main islands.

Nolo’s strongest winds will remain offshore since the hurricane is passing well to the south of the Big Island. Still, tropical storm-force winds stronger than 40 mph are likely in areas of steep terrain on Saturday and hurricane-force gusts stronger than 75 mph can’t be ruled out.

State and county offices, public schools and the University of Hawaii are closed Thursday and Friday on the Big Island and will close Friday on Maui, Gov. Greensaidin a social media post.

Approximately 400 National Guard troops are positioned across the state, with 121 on the Big Island, the governor said inan updateFriday.

County officials have openedshelterson the Big Island. “If your home flooded before, or is at risk, consider moving to safer shelter before the full force of the storm hits,” Hawaii County Mayor Kimo Alameda said in a Wednesday news release. “Because the ground remains saturated, flooding may happen rapidly.”

The state has also secured 100 hotel rooms for Big Island residents who wish to evacuate, Greensaidat a Wednesday news conference. Statewide, hundreds of people are still being housed in hotels after being displaced by earlier natural disasters, including hurricanes Lala and Lowell, Department of Human Services director Joseph Campos said at the same conference.

On Maui, officials have been preparing emergency generators and storm response equipment, and increasing staffing at police and fire departments, the county said in a social mediapost. Bus service will be suspended at different points through the weekend.

Offshore, dangerous seas will build and reach their peak Friday and Saturday. Rough conditions will likely last through the weekend and into next week even as the hurricane starts to track west away from the island Sunday night into Monday.

This year’s super El Nino has helped prime the Pacific to be a factory for strong tropical systems, with extremely warm ocean water and a lack of storm-killing wind shear.

Nolo is one of 19 named storms — including three Category 5 hurricanes — that have roamed the eastern and central Pacific so far and there are two full months of the season left to go. Seventeen originated in the eastern Pacific basin, which typically sees up to 15 storms in an entire season.

For the second time this month, a trio of hurricanes — Nolo, Odalys and Polo — are simultaneously churning in the Pacific.

Polo, which is still roaring off the coast of southern Mexico, is one of five storms this season that have met the criteria forextreme rapid intensification, a wind increase of 58 mph or more in 24 hours.
